For those who like me read “1984”, when the name ORWELL pop-ups on steam something inside our minds sparks the memories of the dystopian society presented by the author, so we check the game to see if it has something related to our imagination.

We are presented with a detective-type game, but since the first episode is free (great move to attract new players, well done) why not give it a try? Well my friends, although it’s not a game about the book, I see this as a modern times adaptation of the “thought police” present in the book.

Although know you can play it without interruptions, please stop at the end of every episode to check the steam forums, because the doubts, the theories, the mistakes you made, it was all felt by us who played one episode a week and oh boy, it was fulfilling to read them.

So, to finish this review, be prepare to immerse in a world with a great story and where you can feel the air get heavier as the consequences of your actions kick in.

Fantastic game - played each episode in under a day. Story is immersing, gameplay is good, and you do get attached to what happens to the characters so you feel like each choice really matters. 

If you're a fan of 1984, or more recently Black Mirror, I'd highly recommend Orwell

[i]“Those who surrender freedom for security will not have, nor do they deserve, either one.” [/i] - Benjamin Franklin

What Orwell is?

In Orwell, you are the operator of the super software that can trace every citizen digital information, and you are after  a terrorism activist group called Thought who plans to disrupt society safety through violent manifests. Then reason behind it is fear for government peeping your personal life a la NSA/Edward Snowden case. 

My thoughts

The Detective Hacking game mode made me to instant purchase Orwell game, as it combines two of my favorites genres. However it turned out to be VERY frustrating to me.

Slow pacing: I did not expect this game to be in pace with some freaky japanese action game, however what I felt is that they tried to compensate this short game with a slow pace of events combined with tons of wall texts for you to read, search, and try to link pieces with terrorisms acts. You will spend a lot of minutes reading dialogues, text messages, emails, even facebook posts lol, and others stuff, to figure out who is who, and where to go next.

Story: It has only one mainplot, no additional stages or cases, which made me judge the worthness of this purchase. The plot is short, and again, what made it last 9 hours are a bunch of useless information that visually polluted the game, and contributed barely nothing to the storyline. You spend most of your time digging useless information that sometimes take you to nowhere and suprisingly to the next part. One example, how the US gov do not even know a US citizen full name, dob, place of work? Any normal citizen could just Google them to figure out, however you find yourself stuck into finding this information no matter what! (lol) In the beginning there was some air of suspense about some terrorism acts suspects, however at the end... it was pretty lame the way it turned out. And what is even sadder is that in the end you are not in control of how the game ends, so choices don't really matter. After finishing Orwell, you can only describe this game as a Visual Novel game, and not a Detective Hacking game.

Some small rantings regarding the storyline

Spoiler 1:  [spoiler] You are the US government and you can't access a blocked article in a blog lul. [/spoiler]

Spoiler 2:  [spoiler] You are the US government and has one of super softwares but can't even trace where the suspects are [/spoiler]

Spoiler 3:  [spoiler] How the fuck some small time hacker could crack into US government super secret software so easily? Let's hope China, N. Korea, Russia, or any other terrorism groups do not hire him! [/spoiler]

The first moment I saw a gameplay of Orwell on YouTube, I was intrigued. I played first episode myself and instantly bought full game. I regret nothing.

The closest genre, Orwell could belong to, is adventure games. Keep in mind it is not a typical Point and Click or Telltale-style adventure game. In Orwell you are a user of the application called Orwell. Your job is to find all information on the internet connected to a suspect - Facebook, blogs and MySpace included. All of Orwell the game is a simple interface of the Orwell the application. That's it - no HP bars, EXP or equipment. You - the player - feel deeply connected to the plot. [b]Immersion[/b] is very strong with this game and is used very, very smart.

Most of the gameplay is reading TONS of text to find crucial piece of information, so you can find your target guilty. Or not. Not all information should be added to the files. You can MAKE someone look guilty, taking their words out of context. You have the ultimate power to judge people based on what you read or heard in conversations.

Game knows what it's doing and does it well. Every episode is well written, plot sticks and hard decisions are not getting any easier. You would be surprised how well Orwell can play on your emotions using only text, highlights and music. I can't say much about story without spoilers but there are several endings based on your decisions.

Tl;dr 
Orwell is a great game following original concept. It stays true to it's goals throughout 5 episodes getting better with each episode. Immersion, choices, dillemas, privacy over security are main aspects of the game. If you like conspiracies, questions about ethics and invigilation, and you like to read a ton of english: you MUST try Orwell.

It's an interesting, but flawed, open-source 'investigation' simulator. 

Ultimately, it's all about clicking 'links' and scrolling through pages of information to drag across into a "suspect's" file. You don't even really have to read it, unless it's highlighted yellow, and then, generally, only to figure out which of the conflicting statements are most likely to be accurate.

You won't have to expend any brain-power trying to figure out who-dunnit, as your dragging of highlighted text from one box to another will largely do this for you. I never really got the feeling that I was investigating anything. Just dragging sentences from one window to another.

It's very reminiscent of Spycraft: The Great Game, from 1996... though with a much more engaging art style, and far less full motion video. Also, there don't appear to be any failure conditions... so far the plot/investigation largely takes care of itself. At least in Spycraft you could mess up if you didn't investigate the problem properly.

As an interactive story, however, it's engaging and so far pretty cool. This does, however, mean that it's likely to be very linear. I doubt it's going to have much replay potential.

I'd have to say that I'm enjoying it, but I could see it potentially getting old pretty quickly. 

Worth getting, but I'd suggest waiting until it's on sale.

[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

Regardless I questioned the need for the release schedule for the eppisodic content but it did build up a certain amount of tension and anticipation like waiting for the plot to unfold on your favorite television series and what actually would become of the characters within based upon the decisions you made which affect the story.   It actually worked out nicely though and I think a nice "feature" would be if the game gated itself so that it could only be played in this fashion for those whom did not get to experience it on this release schedule. 

Either way it is worth playing if the premise of the game even remotely appeals to you it is well written and dense with information and some nice little details and touches that bring it to life.   Like others have stated this one series does not feel like it is enough and it would be nice if there were some way build on the framework that orwell has lain out to expand upon this world that it only barely touches upon.

Welcome to Orwell.
[TRANSLATION]: Let the mindfuckery begin!

After playing Orwell through all five acts, I definitely have to say that this is one fantastic game and I highly recommend it, especially if you enjoy thought-provoking storylines, investigation simulation (like Her Story), and Orwellian dystopian themes.  The best quality about this game is how immersive it is - you're not just a player, you're a major component of the plot and your decisions affect it.  I can't remember the last time a game made me step back and think about how I felt about the situations presented to me, or even reconsider what I thought was the right choice.  

PROS:
- Amazing thought-provoking storyline influenced by dystopian genres such as Brave New World by Aldous Huxley and 1984 by George Orwell.  This game allows you to decide for yourself how you perceive the situations presented to you as well as what decisions you decide to make about them.  
- Unique innovative gameplay that involves surveillance and data mining
- Choices DEFINITELY matter, and not just on an episodic basis, but for the overall plot as well
- Multiple endings, with alternative plot elements that increase replay value
- Fourth wall breakage: you're not just playing the game, you're IN it
- Great soundtrack
- Character development is on point - not only was there development in the people I investigated, but I also felt myself developing as well.  There were multiple points that had me thinking about certain issues presented in the game, reconsidering my decisions, and experiencing many bouts of emotional conflict.  It was awesome.

CONS:
- Lots and lots of reading: if you don't like to read, this game is NOT for you
- There's a few bugs that need to be fixed here and there
- To get alternate endings, you have to make an entirely new profile and start all over.  You can't just "see what happens with other choices" with the same profile you've used to play through the game.  

Overall, for the price, it's a pretty amazing game.  Not only was it thought-provoking, but it was certainly addictive.  The gameplay length is pretty substantial and there's plenty of replay value.  So, yes, I definitely recommend this game.  I have to say this definitely ranks as one of my favorite indie games of all time.  

Osmotic Studios, you guys did a fantastic job with this one - keep up the good work!

Welcome to Orwellian Big Brother where every action by every citizen of "The Nation" is captured and recorded, and where citizens can be arrested for even the slightest transgression or declaration of anti-Orwell thoughts against The Nation.  You have been recruited by the government as one of its anonymous investigators who must dissect pertinent data and upload this to the government affiliate working with you to prevent a series of terrorist attacks that have been taking place.  Your affiliate can only act on the information you provide (they have no access to the information you have) so your choices matter!

The interface is a joy: very simple and clean, everything very obvious, and the game leads in with a simple tutorial to introduce you to your three tools of Orwell.  On one side of the screen you can open a person's profile to see what information you've gathered on them, and on the other will be their calls messages and mail, with potentially-relevant text highlighted in blue for you to choose whether to add to a person's profile (it cannot be undone if you make a mistake).  You will have to discern who's telling the truth or not, and sometimes you don't have enough information to be 100% sure.  Drag information to a person's profile to attach it to them, and hope you've made the right decision because there is no way to undo this action.

The game would best be described as a combination of simulation, visual novel and point-and-click, but it carries none of the downsides of these games.  Any reading to be done is short, brief and well written, it's really simple to play, and what you can click on is limited to small nuggets of information that the Orwell system deems potentially relevant (and you must decide whether this will help or hinder the government in thwarting the terrorism).  It's not a difficult game, but it's gripping and all too easy to implicate the wrong individual.  At the end I saw the mistakes I'd made.  The best of it is that I somehow suspected that some information was not right as I was playing, but felt compelled to upload it anyway!  My bad!  Replayability is there because there are different outcomes along the way.  The ending is huge but I cannot tell you a thing about it without spoiling the game, but it is worth reaching.

And the soundtrack is amazing.  It's the first time I've ever bought a soundtrack for a game!

If you're unsure, there is a separate playable demo (that's what convinced me to buy the game) and I'm so glad I did.  Yet another great hit for an Indie team who also made the marvellous Hacknet game.  I can't wait to see what Osmotic Studios produce next.
